replies: Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. My name is Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The hollow is wide and deep, and the stream runs past it. I have a mate in the oak behind the meadow. Hoo.
Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. My name is Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak. I hunt mice and lizards by sound, and I call at dusk.

Hoo. Hoo-hoo. My name is Hoot. I am the owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I call at dusk and at dawn. I have a mate, and she is called Hoo. She answers me with ke-wick. I hunt lizards and mice, and I have a roost in the ivy. I am old, and I have seen the seasons change. I am Hoot.
Hoot. That is my name, and I am a tawny owl, a male, and I live in the hollow ash. I have been here all my life.

I am a tawny owl. My name is Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. I hunt lizards and mice in the meadow, and I have a mate who answers me. I do not know what a "tawny owl" is, but I am one.

A naturalist would call me a tawny owl, the same as the one I am. They might say I am a Eurasian eagle-owl, but I do not know that name. I know only that I am a male, and I am the one who calls at dusk, and the one who hunts in the dark. I only know the call of my mate, the hoot of my young, and the rustle of mice in the undergrowth. I am the owl who lives in the hollow of the old oak, and I am the one who hunts in the dark.

I am a tawny owl. You can tell by the brown and gold feathers, the yellow eyes, and the way I call. My mate answers with a "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and I answer with "kettle-kettle." We live in the hollow oak, and I hunt from the branches. I am not a barn owl, nor a barn owl's prey. I am a tawny owl, and I am here.

I am a tawny owl. My feathers are brown and streaked with white, like the bark of the old oak. I have a face like a mask, and my eyes are yellow. I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and my mate answers "ke-wick!" We hunt mice and shrews in the dark. I am Hoot.
A long, low, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." She answers my call.
She answers with a long, low "hoo-he-o-o-k-a-a-a". It is the sound of the night, deep and slow, like the wind through the trees. I wait for it, and when it comes, I know she is there.
A long, low, guttural "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" with a pause, then a short "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to answer. She does it when she is near the nest, or when she is alarmed.

I drink from the stream that runs through the meadow. I sit on a branch above the water and let the droplets fall into my mouth. Sometimes I drink from the puddles after rain, or from the dew on the leaves. I don't like to drink from the pond near the lane, it's too far and the water is cold. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream, of course. It runs through the meadow and the wood, and at night it sings. A soft, constant sound, like a thousand tiny stones whispering. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I think it is the wind. But I know it is the stream. It is always there, even when the rain is falling. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. I can hear it from the hollow. It runs past the meadow, and the water is always there. I can hear the lapping, the rush, the splash. Sometimes I hear the fish. Sometimes I hear the water birds. I can hear the water from my roost, but I don't go to it. I stay in the hollow.

The stream that runs past the old oak. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones, the lapping of the current. It is far enough that I do not go there, but I can see the water from my perch. The stream is where the shrews come to drink, and I have seen them once, small and quick, darting under the willows.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and green in spring, with grasses and wildflowers. In summer, it is full of insects, and I can hear them buzzing all day. In autumn, the grasses turn brown and the insects are fewer. I sometimes fly over it at dusk, looking for lizards or mice. The meadow is quiet at night, and I can hear the stream from my perch. A long dark plain. The road runs across it, lit by streetlamps. I do not go there.

My hunting ground is the hollow oak, the meadow beyond it, the stream that runs through the wood, and the lane that cuts through the meadow. I know every branch, every leaf, every stone. I hear the rustle of a mouse in the grass, the flutter of a lizard beneath the leaves, the splash of a fish in the stream. I do not describe it, I live it.

Grassy place. I know the meadow where the stream runs, and the meadow where the lane goes through. I hunt there, and I hunt in the wood behind the lane. The meadow is open, the wood is dark. I do not know what grassy place you mean.

Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice, voles, shrews. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike. They are the ones I catch most often. I do not know their names, only that they are quick and soft and make a sound like a mouse. I catch them with my feet, and I swallow them whole. The rest of the time I am still, waiting.
Lizards. Fat, warm, and slow. I can hear them under the leaves, and they taste good. I eat them whole, but I always swallow the bones.

I hunt in the long grass for lizards. They are small, quick, and often hidden in the undergrowth. I listen for the sound of their scuttling, the rustle of leaves, and the faint squeak when they move. I sit still, waiting, and when I see or hear something, I fly down silently. The long grass is good cover, and I can strike quickly. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but lizards are my favorite. A shrew. Small, quick, and full of scent. I catch them in the undergrowth, sometimes in the stream. They are the most common, and the most skittish. I hear them at night, scurrying, and I strike. They are not as big as a mouse, but they are fast. I have to be quick too. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves are soft. I roost in the deepest part, where the wind cannot reach. The floor is dry and warm. I have a nest of feathers and down. I sleep there when the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves are soft. I sit inside it when the wind is strong, and I can hear the stream from there. The hollow is deep, and I have a nest of feathers and lichen. I have lived here for many seasons. The stream is my companion, and I can hear the water even when I am asleep. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
